Postoperative arrhythmias are common after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery and are linked to adverse outcomes. Colchicine, an anti‐inflammatory agent, has shown inconsistent results in prior studies, possibly due to dosing and timing variations.

Objectives

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of short‐term, weight‐adjusted colchicine initiated preoperatively for preventing postoperative arrhythmias after CABG.

Methods

In this randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial, 172 adults scheduled for on‐pump CABG received colchicine or placebo. The regimen included a preoperative loading dose (1 mg twice daily) followed by a weight‐based maintenance dose (0.5 mg daily if <70 kg; 1 mg daily if ≥70 kg) for 14 days. The primary outcome was incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF). Secondary outcomes included early (≤48 h) and late (>48 h) POAF, other arrhythmias, inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), length of stay, and adverse events.

Results

Of 163 analyzed patients (81 colchicine, 82 placebo), POAF incidence was significantly lower in the colchicine group (17.3% vs. 46.3%; RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.66; p < 0.001), with an absolute risk reduction of 29.0% and number needed to treat (NNT) of 4. Colchicine reduced both early and late POAF (p < 0.001 and p = 0.002). No significant reduction was seen in other arrhythmias. Gastrointestinal events, primarily diarrhea, were more common with colchicine (25.9% vs. 8.5%, p = 0.003), but were manageable and without serious adverse events.

Conclusion

Short‐term perioperative weight‐adjusted colchicine is effective and safe for preventing POAF after CABG, with a low NNT and manageable side effects, though it did not significantly affect other arrhythmias.

Introduction Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) is the most prevalent arrhythmia following cardiac surgery, occurring in 25%–40% of patients after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) procedures. POAF is associated with increased risks of stroke, heart failure, longer intensive care unit and hospital stays, higher healthcare costs, and greater short‐ and long‐term mortality [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ]. The pathogenesis of POAF is multifactorial, involving postoperative inflammation, sympathetic activation, oxidative stress, and atrial structural remodeling [ 6 ]. Given the central role of inflammation, anti‐inflammatory strategies have been investigated for POAF prophylaxis. While corticosteroids are effective, concerns regarding hyperglycemia, impaired wound healing, and infection limit their routine use [ 7 , 8 ]. Colchicine, a well‐established anti‐inflammatory medicine that inhibits microtubule polymerization and the NLRP3 inflammasome, has shown promise in reducing inflammation in cardiovascular conditions like pericarditis and coronary artery disease [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ]. Preliminary studies and meta‐analyses on colchicine for POAF prevention have yielded inconsistent results, with variations in dosing regimens, timing of initiation, and study populations contributing to the controversy [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ]. Therefore, we conducted a randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of a short‐term perioperative weight‐adjusted colchicine regimen for the prevention of postoperative arrhythmias, with a primary focus on POAF, in patients undergoing CABG. Concurrent assessment of inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR) was performed to elucidate potential mechanistic links and prognostic factors. 2. Methods 2.1. Study Design and Participants This was a single‐center, randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial conducted in northern Iran's heart center, between May 2024 and October 2025. The study protocol was approved prior to patient enrollment by the Ethics Committee of Mazandaran University of Medical Sciences and Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (Ethics Code: IR.MAZUMS.REC.1403.161, IRCT20200328046886N6), and all participants provided written informed consent. Adult patients (aged 18–80 years) scheduled for elective on‐pump CABG were eligible. Key exclusion criteria included a history of AF or other sustained arrhythmias, concomitant valvular or other cardiac surgery, severe renal or hepatic impairment, known hypersensitivity to colchicine, use of strong CYP3A4/P‐glycoprotein inhibitors and recent use of corticosteroids and antiarrhythmic drugs within a month. 2.2. Randomization and Blinding Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive colchicine or an identical‐appearing placebo. Randomization was performed using a computer‐generated sequence with block sizes of 4, managed via the sealedenvelope.com online service. The randomization list was kept by the hospital pharmacy, which prepared the sequentially numbered, identical drug packages. Patients, treating physicians, surgeons, anesthesiologists, and all outcomes assessors were blinded to group assignment to minimize assessment bias. 2.3. Intervention Patients in the colchicine group received a loading dose of 1 mg orally twice daily on the day before surgery. Postoperatively, they received a maintenance dose of 0.5 mg daily if body weight was <70 kg, or 1 mg daily if weight was ≥70 kg, continued for a total of 14 days. The placebo group received matching tablets on an identical schedule. All patients received standard perioperative care, including beta‐blockers (unless contraindicated), statins, and thromboprophylaxis, according to institutional guidelines (Figure 1 ). This study was conducted in compliance with the ethical standards of the responsible institution on human subjects as well as with the Helsinki Declaration. FIGURE 1. Outcomes The primary efficacy outcome was the incidence of any documented episode of POAF (defined as AF lasting ≥30 s) within the first 14 days after surgery. All patients were monitored using continuous telemetry cardiac monitoring during their ICU and subsequent all wards stay, until discharge. Also, daily clinical assessments and needed confirmatory 12‐lead ECG recordings were performed. For those who needed to complete their 2 weeks monitoring beyond hospitalization, 24‐h Holter rhythm monitoring was performed. After discharge, patients were systematically followed through scheduled clinically visits or telephone contact up to 3 months. Secondary outcomes included: incidence of early POAF (≤48 h post‐op) and late POAF (>48 h post‐op); duration of POAF episodes; incidence of other documented arrhythmias, including premature ventricular contractions (PVCs), premature atrial contractions (PACs), ventricular blocks, tachycardia, and bradycardia; levels of inflammatory markers (C‐reactive protein [CRP] and erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR]) measured preoperatively and on postoperative day 7; length of stay in the ICU and hospital; rate of readmission; and incidence of serious and non‐serious adverse events. 2.5. Statistical Analysis The sample size was calculated based on published POAF rates of approximately 30% after isolated CABG surgery. The planned effect size was an absolute reduction of 20% (from 30% in the control arm to 10% in the colchicine arm). This assumption, together with α = 0.05, power = 80%, and a 1:1 randomization ratio, yielded a required sample size of 172 patients (78 patients per group) after accounting for an anticipated 10% attrition rate. A sample size of 172 (86 per group) was enrolled. To further assess the robustness of the primary endpoint, we calculated the fragility index. The primary analysis was conducted using a modified intention‐to‐treat approach. A per‐protocol analysis was also performed as a sensitivity analysis. Data were analyzed using SPSS v23 software. Categorical variables were compared using Chi‐square or Fisher's exact test. Continuous variables were compared using independent t‐test or Mann–Whitney U test as appropriate. The relative risk (RR), absolute risk reduction (ARR), and number needed to treat (NNT) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for the primary outcome. A two‐sided p ‐value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. To address baseline imbalances, a multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed. 3. Results 3.1. Patient Characteristics A total of 473 patients were assessed for eligibility, of whom 172 were randomized. Patients were allocated to colchicine ( n = 86) or placebo ( n = 86). A total of 163 patients completed the study protocol (81 in the colchicine group and 82 in the placebo group). Nine patients did not complete the study protocol. The study flow is shown in (Figure 2 ). The baseline demographic, clinical, and surgical characteristics were well‐balanced between the two groups, except for a higher prevalence of diabetes in the placebo group (75.6% vs. 56.8%, p = 0.011) and more frequent opioid use in the colchicine group (12.3% vs. 2.4%, p = 0.015). Baseline medication use, including beta‐blockers and statins, was balanced between groups (Table 1 ). Background amiodarone prophylaxis and magnesium supplementation were not used. FIGURE 2. Primary Outcome: Incidence of POAF The primary outcome occurred in 14 patients (17.3%) in the colchicine group and 38 patients (46.3%) in the placebo group (Relative Risk [RR] 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.66; p < 0.001). The ARR was 29.0% (95% CI 15.5%–42.5%), resulting in a NNT of 4. 3.3. Secondary Outcomes Colchicine significantly reduced both early‐onset (≤48 h) and late‐onset (>48 h) POAF. The incidence of early POAF was 8.6% versus 36.6% ( p < 0.001), and of late POAF was 9.9% versus 29.3% ( p = 0.002). Patients in the colchicine group also had fewer days with early and late AF (Table 2 ). While colchicine significantly reduced POAF, its effect on other postoperative arrhythmias was not significant. Rates of PVCs, PACs, ventricular blocks, tachycardia, and bradycardia did not differ between the colchicine and placebo groups (all p > 0.05, Table 2 ), suggesting that the antiarrhythmic effect of colchicine may be specific to atrial fibrillation (AF) in the postoperative setting. Consequently, our findings on secondary outcomes such as length of hospital stay and ICU stay, hospital readmission, fatality, bleeding episodes and thromboembolic events were not statistically significant. Safety and Adverse Events The most common adverse event was diarrhea, which occurred significantly more often in the colchicine group (25.9% vs. 8.5%, p = 0.003). Gastrointestinal adverse events were predominantly mild (Grade 1). Among the 21 patients with diarrhea in the colchicine group, 3 (3.7%) required temporary dose reduction, and 2 (2.5%) discontinued the study medication. No cases of severe (Grade 3/4) diarrhea were reported. Rates of nausea/vomiting, infection, acute kidney injury, neurologic complications, and bleeding were not significantly different between the groups (Table 4 ). No serious adverse events (e.g., severe myelosuppression, rhabdomyolysis, or death) were attributed to the study drug. TABLE 4. Selected adverse events. Subgroup Analyses The beneficial effect of colchicine was consistent across key subgroups. In patients with diabetes, POAF incidence was 20.0% versus 50.0% ( p = 0.002). In patients aged ≥65 years, POAF incidence was 19.4% versus 51.2% ( p = 0.005). Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to adjust for potential confounders, including diabetes mellitus, age, and baseline CRP levels. Colchicine remained independently associated with a significantly lower risk of POAF (adjusted OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.15–0.64, p = 0.002). Diabetes mellitus (adjusted OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.01–3.12, p = 0.046), increasing age (adjusted OR 1.03 per year, 95% CI 1.00–1.06, p = 0.041), and higher baseline CRP (adjusted OR 1.02 per mg/L, 95% CI 1.01–1.04, p = 0.008) were independently associated with increased risk of POAF. The model demonstrated good calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.62) and acceptable explanatory power (Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.28). A per‐protocol analysis was performed as a sensitivity analysis and yielded results consistent with the primary findings. Although 163 patients completed the study (94.7% of the planned 172), the achieved power remained >95% due to the larger‐than‐expected observed treatment effect (29% absolute reduction). Robustness was assessed via the fragility index and consistency across analyses. 4. Discussion The underlying mechanisms through which colchicine exerts its preventive effects on post‐CABG arrhythmias are not fully elucidated. However, several potential mechanisms have been proposed, including its anti‐inflammatory properties, inhibition of fibrosis, vasodilatory effects, and modulation of ion channels [ 10 , 13 , 17 , 18 ]. In this randomized controlled trial, a short‐term weight‐adjusted perioperative regimen of colchicine significantly reduced the risk of POAF following CABG surgery by approximately 63% relative to placebo, with a low NNT of 4, indicating a clinically meaningful effect superior to that reported for standard prophylaxis. The protective effect was observed in both early (≤48 h) and late (>48 h) postoperative periods. Importantly, colchicine remained independently associated with reduced POAF after adjustment for baseline imbalances, including diabetes, age, and CRP levels, supporting the robustness and internal validity of the findings. Our findings align with the biological rationale targeting postoperative inflammation, a key driver of atrial remodeling and arrhythmogenesis in POAF. Colchicine's anti‐inflammatory action, primarily through inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome and microtubule disruption, likely attenuates the inflammatory cascade triggered by surgical trauma and cardiopulmonary bypass. The observed association between higher baseline inflammatory markers (CRP and ESR) and increased POAF incidence further supports this hypothesis [ 6 , 9 ]. The optimal dosing and duration of colchicine for preventing POAF remain uncertain. Previous studies have used varying regimens, leading to inconsistent results [ 10 , 15 , 16 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ]. In our study, a short‐term, weight‐adjusted regimen initiated preoperatively was effective, suggesting that achieving therapeutic levels before the inflammatory insult of surgery may be critical. Our results contribute to resolving inconsistencies in prior literature. While the COPPS trial demonstrated a reduction in POAF with colchicine, COPPS‐2 and the END‐AF trials reported less consistent benefits, potentially due to differences in study design, dosing, and tolerability [ 10 , 13 , 15 , 16 , 22 ]. Notably, our study differs by employing a preoperative loading dose, followed by weight adjusted maintenance dose combined with a shorter duration of therapy, which may enhance efficacy while limiting cumulative toxicity [ 14 ]. Similarly, the COCS trial reported mixed findings, highlighting the importance of regimen optimization [ 19 ] (Table 5 ). TABLE 5. Postoperatively, maintenance dose of 0.5 mg daily if body weight was <70 kg, or 1 mg daily if weight was ≥70 kg 14 days POAF↓ Other arrhythmia, Not Significant Open in a new tab Our study revealed significant differences in clinical outcomes between the colchicine and placebo groups. Patients receiving colchicine demonstrated a lower incidence of early AF within 48 h ( p < 0.001), fewer days with early AF ( p < 0.001), reduced late AF episodes ( p = 0.002), and shorter duration of AF ( p = 0.003). Total POAF was also significantly reduced ( p < 0.001). However, no significant differences were observed in other postoperative arrhythmias, secondary outcomes such as length of hospital and ICU stay and thromboembolic events, suggesting that colchicine's antiarrhythmic effect may be specific to AF, which is more strongly driven by inflammatory mechanisms. While Inflammatory markers, including CRP and ESR, did not differ significantly between treatment groups at baseline or follow‐up, a marginal reduction in follow‐up markers was observed in the Colchicine group. However, patients who developed POAF had significantly higher baseline levels of these markers. CRP and ESR were elevated in those with early AF, late AF, and overall POAF, suggesting that baseline inflammatory status may play a prognostic role. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the multifactorial nature of POAF. Colchicine offers a low‐cost, highly effective and accessible therapeutic option compared to conventional antiarrhythmic agents [ 23 ]. Its perioperative use, particularly when initiated before surgery, may optimize its therapeutic effect. The ARR of 29.0% observed in our study is consistent with prior meta‐analyses, and the low NNT highlights its potential clinical utility. However, direct comparisons with other prophylactic strategies should be interpreted cautiously. Also, no significant differences were observed in length of ICU stay, hospital stay, readmission, bleeding episodes, TIA and infectious complications suggesting that the clinical impact beyond arrhythmia prevention may be limited in the short term. The safety profile of colchicine observed in this study is consistent with previous trials [ 17 , 18 , 24 ]. Gastrointestinal adverse events, particularly diarrhea, were significantly more frequent in the colchicine group (25.9% vs. 8.5%). These events were generally mild to moderate and rarely required treatment discontinuation. Other adverse events were comparable between groups, and no serious drug‐related complications were observed. However, rare adverse events, such as myopathy and Leucopenia, have been reported in some cases. Our findings indicate that colchicine's benefit appears largely specific to POAF, with no significant effect on other arrhythmias such as PVCs, PACs, or bradycardia. This may reflect differing underlying mechanisms, as non‐AF arrhythmias are more influenced by factors such as autonomic imbalance, ischemia, or electrolyte disturbances. Alternatively, the study may have been underpowered to detect differences in less frequent arrhythmias. Limitations include Single‐center design, short follow‐up (14 days). Incomplete lab data, and imbalance in diabetes prevalence between groups may have influenced outcomes, although adjusted analyses were performed. Overall, colchicine appears to be a viable and safe strategy for POAF prevention. We suggest further studies consider Troponin I or T levels (pre‐op and post‐op), Inflammatory Cytokines (IL‐6, TNF‐α, IL‐1β), major adverse cardiac events (MACE), readmission rate (30‐day or 90‐day), atrial effective refractory period (AERP) or electrophysiological parameters (if available). 5. Conclusion Perioperative administration of colchicine is a highly effective, well‐tolerated, and low‐cost strategy for the prevention of AF after CABG surgery, with a NNT of only 4. Its effect appears specific to POAF, with no significant impact on other postoperative arrhythmias in this trial. The increased risk of manageable gastrointestinal side effects warrants dose individualization and careful patient selection. These findings support the consideration of colchicine as a routine or alternative prophylactic agent against POAF, particularly in high‐risk subgroups. Future multi‐center studies with extended follow‐up are warranted to assess long‐term outcomes and refine dosing strategies.
